A dynamic (occupancy) ordered-beta model for percent-cover resurvey data

This document reanalyses the data of

Wessely, J. et al. (2026). Rising plant extinction rates on European mountain summits. Science 393, 1021–1026. doi:10.1126/science.aed2974

Published 3 September 2026

1. Introduction

Wessely et al. resurveyed 896 permanent plots on 62 European mountain summits in 16 regions, four times between 2001 and 2022. They define a local extinction as a species recorded at one survey but not re-recorded at the next, which they count at the level of plots, summits and regions. From those counts they report that extinction rates have risen across surveys, and attribute that rise to climate warming.

In this reanalysis, I will consider local extinction to occur only when a species disappears from a summit (strictly, from the part of it that its plots sample), as I choose to believe that even local extinction does not happen that locally. I will frequently (and hopefully consistently) distinguish between local extinction and apparent loss, and between colonisation and apparent colonisation. Local extinction is when a species no longer occupies the summit. Apparent loss is when the species was recorded at one survey and not at the next. Apparent loss is driven by more than local extinction. It is also driven by the processes that drive cover, and by detectability. Colonistion is when a species becomes an occupant, either after local extinction or because it is new. Apparent colonisation is when a species recorded after an absence may have been there all along, but was previously not observed.

Wessely et al. discuss this difference, but do not model it. They apply a 12.1% correction for absences inflated by the change in sampling method at the third and fourth surveys (see the supplementary information), and note that 34.2% of the plot-level apparent losses at the second and third surveys were followed by re-observation at a later survey (p. 1021), so that a more conservative estimate of local extinction is presence at the first survey and absence from all consecutive surveys (a history of 1,0,0,01,0,0,0, their “conservative accounting”). I will refer to their transition count as
the liberal accounting.

They fit binomial generalised linear mixed-effects models to the data of any history with a change to absence, with year or exposure to warming as the predictor and random effects for region, summit, plot, and model the number of apparent colonisations in the same way. I purposefully did not write local extinction, as Wessely et al. study local extinction by analysing apparent loss, and will make the point that local extinction should not be studied from apparent loss.

In order to successfully infer local extinction from patterns in apparent loss directly, a few assumptions need to hold:

  1. species are homogeneous in detectability, in their response to warming, and in their extinction rates;
  2. imperfect detection arises from sampling effort alone;
  3. apparent loss follows the same warming effect as local extinction; and
  4. the number of species recorded equals the number present (similar to 2.).

Some of these Wessely et al. themselves note not to hold: “we do not know whether the species persisted on the same summit or in the same region outside of the surveyed plots” (p. 1021), and “part of the local extinctions reported certainly result from species that were overlooked or from natural fluctuation” (p. 1025).

Violating these assumptions has the following consequences:

  • species richness is deflated. Fewer species are recorded than are actually present;
  • the rate of local extinction is inflated. A recorded 1,01,0 is either a real loss or a species present and missed, so the probability of apparent loss (which is what the authors study) is an upper bound on local extinction;
  • counts of local extinction are biased up and/or down depending on the history considered. A species that persists but is missed is counted as lost, while a species missed at the first survey cannot be counted as lost, so its extinction goes uncounted (and if it is seen later, it looks like a colonisation);
  • the warming slope of apparent loss is not that of local extinction. Whether a species is recorded depends on its cover, and cover responds to warming, so the slope of apparent loss reflects the extinction response and the species’ cover responses;
  • uncertainty is underestimated. Fitting a (univariate) regression of richness requires homogeneity of species, which is ecologically unrealistic. It requires assuming all species respond similarly to the environment, i.e., it severely underfits the data, leading to overly optimistic conclusions. Similarly, apparent loss of species depends on their environmental preferences, so assuming all species change to absence with the same probability will underestimate statistical uncertainty.

Species richness, local extinction and cover share the same study design, and thus suffer from similar problems, so agreement between analyses would not be corroboration, but at best signal the same problem. Because the number of apparently lost species is a consequence of local extinction, species richness and cover, disentangling these processes requires a joint model rather than separate analyses. Studied separately from cover, apparent loss discards information in cover that helps separate it from extinction. I do not blame the concept of separate analyses of the same data on Wessely et al. though, as most of community ecology still does not fit joint models where needed.

In a different analysis, Wessely et al. model apparent loss at the fourth survey as a function of cover change between the first and third surveys. They note that low cover at the first survey increases “the probability of both subsequent local extinctions and observation errors” (p. 1023). However, if cover is a function of warming, then naturally so is apparent loss. Apparent loss can then be predicted by change in cover, not because cover affects local extinction but because apparent loss is inherently a function of the processes that drive cover. This becomes clearer in the dynamic occupancy model presented below.

To estimate the effects of warming on local extinction, and assess the consequences of inferring local extinction from apparent loss directly, I construct a joint model. Section 2 presents the GLORIA data, section 3 the joint model for cover, occupancy, local extinction and colonisation that relaxes some of the assumptions above, and section 4 presents the results. Section 5 uses simulations on the basis of the fitted model to further study how the effects of warming on cover impact the effect of warming on apparent loss.

2. The data

All analyses here use the authors’ data and warming covariate, with the exception of the warming data used to predict cover. The data from the paper is deposited at doi:10.5061/dryad.vmcvdnd6v.

The data includes 721 vascular plant species across 896 plots, each plot visited at all 4 surveys. There are up to 16 plots per summit, and 62 summits in 16 regions. The data is relatively sparse, so I kept only species with at least five occurrences, 549 of the 721. This is a relatively liberal threshold. From five occurrences it is barely possible to estimate species-specific intercepts, let alone responses to altitude or warming. The threshold matters little for extinction, as it is assumed common to all species (section 3).

Sampling effort changed during the study, as a frequency method was applied in the first two surveys, not in the third, and partly in the fourth. In the frequency method, each plot is divided into 100 subplots of 10 × 10 cm and the presence of every species is recorded in each. That means the cover data is not true cover data, but represents proportions calculated from a binomial response. As I do not have access to the original data, I here have to assume it is a continuous measure of relative abundance. In the fourth survey, the frequency method was used at 691 of the 896 plots.

The warming covariate

Warming in Wessely et al. is represented as the difference between mean temperature over the 14 years preceding a survey and the 1900–1950 mean, from the Climatic Research Unit version 4.06, downscaled to 100 m. Version 4.06 ends in 2021 and so has no data for the last survey in 2022, which is fine if you only look at transitions and represent the warming during a transition by the warming at its start. As a consequence, I used both v4.06 and v4.10: the former for initial occupancy, local extinction and colonisation, as in Wessely et al., and the latter to model cover as a function of warming. Across the 62 summits and 3 transitions the two agree at r=0.94r = 0.94, ranging from 0.87 to 0.95 by transition, with a mean absolute difference of 0.09 °C.

Of the 186 summit-transition values, the covariate takes only 74 distinct ones. In 5 of the 16 regions every summit has the same trajectory. So the covariate is effectively a region effect plus a survey effect.

Centring

I centred and scaled the covariate to improve convergence (standard practice). Centring on the grand mean would make the intercept of local extinction the rate at average warming across all summits and transitions, which is not particularly useful here.

Centring within survey could be useful, so that each transition’s mean warming is represented by a survey-specific intercept. However, there was not quite enough evidence to support survey-specific local extinction rates, and survey-specific centring would have made the global intercept harder to interpret.

Centring on the first survey’s mean warming is what I went with, as it represents warming already present in 2001, about 0.79 °C above the 1900–1950 baseline.

Altitude was centred on its mean and scaled, so the cover intercept is the cover of a species at mean altitude.

Transition patterns

Occupancy occurs at the summit-species-transition level, so that there are 102,114 transitions in the data. Checking the transitions against the data at the summit-level:

pattern nn % of all transitions
detected, detected 4,822 4.72
detected, all zero 364 0.36
all zero, detected 440 0.43
all zero, all zero 96,488 94.49

so 94% of transitions are continued absence, and 5,186 begin from a presence.

Covariate replication within species

Both covariates are constant within summit. Altitude has one value per summit, and the warming that initial occupancy responds to is one value per summit, that of the first survey. The median species occupies two summits, so there is little information to estimate species-specific responses to the predictors from. From the species kept with sufficient presences, 326 of 549 species have at least two distinct warming values and 399 have at least two altitude values, but only 325 have both, and only 124 have the possibility to support a species-specific quadratic response to the predictors.

I thus decided to provide a species its own slope parameter when it had at least two distinct values of the covariate, and its own quadratic term when it had four. For species that did not have enough observations I pooled the parameters to a common value, so that they could be retained in the analysis. Warming in the cover model varies also temporally, so that species-specific effects could be estimated from spatial or temporal replication alone, and species received a common slope under similar conditions.

Distinct covariate values among the summits where each species occurs, for species with at least five occurrences. Red: too few for a slope. Orange: enough for a linear altitude term but not a quadratic.

3. A joint model for occupancy and cover

The model has four components: cover (how much of a species there is) in a plot at a survey, initial occupancy (whether a species occupies a summit at the first survey), and local extinction and colonisation (how occupancy changes from one survey to the next). Occupancy models usually model abundance or presence, but cover being a form of relative abundance, the occupancy framework is straightforwardly adjusted to incorporate it. Note, occupancy is latent and needs to be estimated at the summit level, unlike cover and presence and absence that are observed.

Cover (between 0% and 100%), absence due to lack of cover (0%) and full cover (100%) are modelled with an ordered beta distribution, with a linear predictor per species and plot. The same process that generates non-zero cover then also represents lack of cover, so species whose expected cover is low also have a larger chance of being recorded as zero. The predictor holds species-specific intercepts, altitude terms and warming, as well as intercepts for survey, for the (lack of) frequency method, and cut-off parameters that represent the detection threshold, also as a function of survey intercepts and frequency method.

Initial occupancy has species-specific intercepts and warming terms, with random intercepts for region and summit shared across species. After the first survey, occupancy changes through extinction and colonisation rates that depend on warming and carry their own region and summit random intercepts. The rates are offset by the duration of a transition, so a longer transition generates more extinctions and colonisations. Both local extinction and colonisation are assumed to be the same for all species, which is probably not realistic, but the data is too sparse for species-specific rates.

The probability of apparent loss for a species jj recorded on summit mm from survey s−1s-1 to ss is

(1−ϕm,s−1)+ϕm,s−1∏i=1nmpmisj0, (1-\phi_{m,s-1}) + \phi_{m,s-1}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} p^0_{misj},

where ϕm,s−1\phi_{m,s-1} is the probability that it persists and pmisj0p^0_{misj} the probability of an absence due to lack of cover in plot ii, one of the nmn_m plots on the summit.

The cover model is constrained to explain, well, cover, so it can only generate more zeros in response to the environment by reducing cover. A species with high expected cover that has become absent thus carries more information on extinction. A species with low cover is more likely to be missed than to have gone extinct, so it carries less information on extinction. Here, I assume that the plots of a summit are independent as there is no information in the data to assume otherwise.

I fitted the model with RTMB, where the random effects are integrated out of the likelihood with the Laplace approximation. Further details on the model, including the derived quantities used in section 4, are hidden below.

Model details

Throughout, ii is a plot, mm a summit, ss a survey, jj a species, and rr the region containing summit mm. There are RR regions, MM summits, JJ species, TT surveys, and nmn_m plots on summit mm. So ymisjy_{misj} is the cover of species jj in plot ii at survey ss, and zmsjz_{msj} the occupancy of a species at a summit mm at survey ss. Δms\Delta_{ms} is the number of years from survey ss to s+1s+1, wmsw_{ms} the warming at the start of a transition, w̃ms\tilde w_{ms} the warming at survey ss used for cover (see The warming covariate), and ϕms\phi_{ms} the probability of persistence.

Cover

Conditional on occupancy, I assume cover follows an ordered-beta distribution (Kubinec 2023; Korhonen et al. 2024), parameterised with mean and precision. Here, it is effectively a zero-inflated beta distribution whose zero probability and mean share one linear predictor. Two (species-specific) cut-offs ζ0j<ζ1j\zeta_{0j} < \zeta_{1j} shift the linear predictor for absences and full cover. As such, additional intercepts δmisζ\delta^{\zeta}_{mis} move the detection threshold for surveys and the frequency method. With the linear predictor ηmisjμ=𝐱mis⊤βμj\eta^\mu_{misj} = \mathbf{x}_{mis}^\top \beta_{\mu j}, the conditional likelihood, whose density is written f(ymisj)f\!\left(y_{misj}\right) below, is

ymisj∣zmsj=1∼{0with probability pmisj0Beta(μmisj,κ)with probability 1−pmisj0−pmisj11with probability pmisj1 y_{misj} \mid z_{msj} = 1 \;\sim\; \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } p^{0}_{misj}\\[4pt] \mathrm{Beta}\!\left(\mu_{misj},\; \kappa\right) & \text{with probability } 1 - p^{0}_{misj} - p^{1}_{misj}\\[4pt] 1 & \text{with probability } p^{1}_{misj} \end{cases}

where

μmisj=logit−1(ηmisjμ),pmisj0=logit−1(ζ0j+δmisζ−ηmisjμ),pmisj1=1−logit−1(ζ1j+δmisζ−ηmisjμ). \mu_{misj} = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\eta^\mu_{misj}\right), \qquad p^{0}_{misj} = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\zeta_{0j} + \delta^{\zeta}_{mis} - \eta^\mu_{misj}\right), \qquad p^{1}_{misj} = 1 - \mathrm{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\zeta_{1j} + \delta^{\zeta}_{mis} - \eta^\mu_{misj}\right).

The beta distribution is written in its mean-precision form Beta(μ,κ)\mathrm{Beta}(\mu, \kappa), with shape parameters μκ\mu\kappa and (1−μ)κ(1-\mu)\kappa, mean μ\mu and variance μ(1−μ)/(1+κ)\mu(1-\mu)/(1+\kappa), so κ\kappa is the precision.

The linear predictor ηmisjμ\eta^\mu_{misj} includes species-specific intercepts, altitude and altitude squared, warming, and intercepts shared across species to accommodate differences in total recorded cover between surveys and between sampling methods:

ηmisjμ=βμ0j+δsμ+δFμFmis+βμ1jaltm+βμ2jaltm2+βμ3jw̃ms,δ1μ=0, \eta^\mu_{misj} = \beta_{\mu 0 j} + \delta^{\mu}_{s} + \delta^{\mu}_{F}\,F_{mis} + \beta_{\mu 1 j}\,\mathrm{alt}_m + \beta_{\mu 2 j}\,\mathrm{alt}_m^2 + \beta_{\mu 3 j}\,\tilde{w}_{ms}, \qquad \delta^{\mu}_1 = 0,

where Fmis=1F_{mis} = 1 when the frequency method was not applied at plot ii at survey ss.

Species intercepts are treated as random effects βμ0j∼N(μμ0,σμ02)\beta_{\mu 0 j} \sim N(\mu_{\mu_0}, \sigma^2_{\mu_0}), to leverage partial pooling for species with few observations. The slopes for altitude and warming are fixed effects.

The detection threshold

I assume that the sampling method could have affected both cover and the detection threshold. For the former, there are species-common intercepts in ηmisjμ\eta^{\mu}_{misj}. The detection threshold is represented by the lower cut-off ζ0j\zeta_{0j}. It is treated as a random effect, to leverage partial pooling of species, with species-common mean effects

ζ0j∼N(μζ0,σζ02),δmisζ=δsζ+δFζFmis,δ1ζ=0, \zeta_{0j} \;\sim\; N\!\left(\mu_{\zeta_0},\; \sigma_{\zeta_0}^2\right), \qquad \delta^{\zeta}_{mis} \;=\; \delta^{\zeta}_{s} + \delta^{\zeta}_{F}\,F_{mis}, \qquad \delta^{\zeta}_1 = 0,

with FmisF_{mis} as above, so it is constant within each of the first three surveys and splits the plots of the fourth. A positive intercept then raises the probability of an absence.

The upper cut-off is not estimated, due to a lack of data. There are only 2 observations with 100% cover, which is not enough to estimate it. Being unable to estimate the upper cut-off is common in community ecological data, in my experience. With it fixed, the model is practically a zero-inflated beta distribution, but where the two components share a linear predictor.

Precision

I assume a single precision parameter across all species, as there was too little information in the data to estimate species-specific precision parameters, even when leveraging partial pooling as for the intercepts.

The plot random effect

Altitude is recorded at summit level and constant across the plots of a summit, and similarly for warming. Without a plot-level term, nothing in the cover model varies between the plots of a summit at a given survey, apart from the sampling method at the fourth.

A plot effect on ηmisjμ\eta^{\mu}_{misj} allows for heterogeneity in cover or absence within summits, but there is not enough information for a species-specific effect, and there are no plot-level covariates. A plot random effect shared across all species is possible, but it comes at a considerable computational cost, because there are many plots, so the fit goes from running in a few hours to a few days. The reported results are without the plot random effect. I fitted a model with the plot random effect as a check, and it changed little. The random effect had a standard deviation of 0.42 on the logit scale of cover, the warming effect on extinction moved from 0.42 (SE 0.16) to 0.35 (SE 0.14), and extinction per transition and richness barely changed.

The cover model

There is no separate observation model, so the processes that drive the cover distribution here are a combination of detection and ecological signal due to cover. This was the main reason I chose to include survey- and frequency intercepts for cover and for the lower cut-off parameter.

That means the cut-off parameters carry most of the observation process that does not vary with the environment. As I have no other information on effort, observers, or otherwise, if detection varies with the environment, it is thus confounded with species responses to warming and altitude. I do not see a way to improve that, given the lack of information and the sparsity of the data.

Rare species are naturally harder to detect, so detectability probably differs between species. That caveat applies both to my model and to the analysis of Wessely et al., and a more complete model for the detection threshold, for example with information about observers, could further improve the analysis.

Initial occupancy

Occupancy at the first survey is

zm1j∼Bernoulli(ψmj),logit(ψmj)=βψ0j+βψ1jwm1+βψ2jwm12+urψ+vmψ, z_{m1j} \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\psi_{mj}), \qquad \mathrm{logit}(\psi_{mj}) = \beta_{\psi 0 j} + \beta_{\psi 1 j}\,w_{m1} + \beta_{\psi 2 j}\,w_{m1}^{2} + u^{\psi}_r + v^{\psi}_{m},

where wm1w_{m1} is the warming of summit mm at the first survey.

The quadratic term is included because a previous model without it reproduced the richness–warming relationship badly, as the region and summit random intercepts absorbed it instead, throwing off the predictions by the model.

βψ0j\beta_{\psi 0 j} is a random species-specific intercept, again using partial pooling. The warming predictor is treated as fixed effect, with again species-specific responses where the data allows for it, and common for species where it does not. urψu^{\psi}_r is a region random intercept and vmψv^{\psi}_{m} a summit-specific random intercept (i.e., (1|region/summit)), both shared across species

urψ∼N(0,σψ,region2),r=1,…,R,vmψ∼N(0,σψ,summit2),m=1,…,M. u^{\psi}_r \;\sim\; N\!\left(0,\; \sigma_{\psi,\mathrm{region}}^2\right), \quad r = 1,\dots,R, \qquad v^{\psi}_m \;\sim\; N\!\left(0,\; \sigma_{\psi,\mathrm{summit}}^2\right), \quad m = 1,\dots,M.

The random intercepts absorb between-region and between-summit (within-region) differences in occupancy.

Extinction and colonisation

Change in occupancy from the first survey to consecutive surveys is fully determined by extinction and colonisation rates λmsext\lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}_{ms} and λmscol\lambda^{\mathrm{col}}_{ms}, which are summit- and survey-specific (due to warming). Both get a linear predictor on the log scale, denoted ηext\eta^{\mathrm{ext}} and ηcol\eta^{\mathrm{col}}:

ηmsext=β0ext+β1extwms+urext+vmext,λmsext=exp(ηmsext),ηmscol=β0col+β1colwms+urcol+vmcol,λmscol=exp(ηmscol),\begin{align*} \eta^{\mathrm{ext}}_{ms} &= \beta^{\mathrm{ext}}_0 + \beta^{\mathrm{ext}}_1 w_{ms} + u^{\mathrm{ext}}_r + v^{\mathrm{ext}}_{m}, \qquad \lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}_{ms} = \exp\!\left(\eta^{\mathrm{ext}}_{ms}\right),\\ \eta^{\mathrm{col}}_{ms} &= \beta^{\mathrm{col}}_0 + \beta^{\mathrm{col}}_1 w_{ms} + u^{\mathrm{col}}_r + v^{\mathrm{col}}_{m}, \qquad \lambda^{\mathrm{col}}_{ms} = \exp\!\left(\eta^{\mathrm{col}}_{ms}\right), \end{align*}

where urext,urcolu^{\mathrm{ext}}_r, u^{\mathrm{col}}_r are again region and vmext,vmcolv^{\mathrm{ext}}_{m}, v^{\mathrm{col}}_{m} summit random intercepts, entering the extinction and colonisation rates

urext∼N(0,σext,region2),vmext∼N(0,σext,summit2),urcol∼N(0,σcol,region2),vmcol∼N(0,σcol,summit2). u^{\mathrm{ext}}_r \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{ext,region}}\right),\quad v^{\mathrm{ext}}_m \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{ext,summit}}\right),\quad u^{\mathrm{col}}_r \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{col,region}}\right),\quad v^{\mathrm{col}}_m \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{col,summit}}\right).

Over a transition of Δms\Delta_{ms} years, ϕms\phi_{ms} is the probability that no extinction event has occurred on a summit that was occupied at survey ss (i.e., persistence), and γms\gamma_{ms} is the probability that at least one colonisation has occurred on a summit that was not occupied

ϕms=exp(−λmsextΔms),γms=1−exp(−λmscolΔms). \phi_{ms} = \exp\!\left(-\lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}_{ms}\,\Delta_{ms}\right), \qquad \gamma_{ms} = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\lambda^{\mathrm{col}}_{ms}\,\Delta_{ms}\right).

This means that the rates are constant within a transition, so the annual risk of extinction does not depend on how long the species has been present, nor on where in the transition I look. e−λmsexte^{-\lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}_{ms}} is annual persistence and 1−exp(−λmsext)1-\exp(-\lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}_{ms}) the annual extinction probability. Because 1−ϕms1-\phi_{ms} increases with Δms\Delta_{ms}, a detected-then-undetected history across ten years is weaker evidence of a high extinction rate than observed across five years.

The coefficients in the above rates are what I am interested in; in particular, β1ext\beta^{\mathrm{ext}}_1 is the change in the log extinction rate due to warming.

Note that although the rates of local extinction and colonisation are the same for all species, occupancy is not, due to species-specific occupancy at the first survey, and apparent loss additionally due to species-specific estimates from the cover model.

Conditional on occupancy, the count of species lost at a summit mm during transition ss is binomial, since every occupant species is lost with the same probability 1−ϕms1-\phi_{ms}. That follows from the simplifying assumption of an extinction rate common to all species (otherwise it would have been Poisson-binomial distributed). I considered species-specific extinction rates, through intercepts or warming slopes, but quickly rejected the idea due to the sparsity of the data. A species trait covariate, such as a thermal preference index, would let the rate vary without needing a single parameter per species, but I do not have access to that at the time of writing.

Likelihood

Joint likelihood

The joint probability of the data and occupancy 𝐳mj=(zm1j,…,zmTj)\mathbf{z}_{mj} = (z_{m1j},\dots,z_{mTj}) is

Lmj=p(𝐲mj,𝐳mj)=p(zm1j)∏s=2Tp(zmsj∣zm,s−1,j)∏s=1Tp(𝐲msj∣zmsj), L_{mj} = p\!\left(\mathbf{y}_{mj}, \mathbf{z}_{mj}\right) = p(z_{m1j})\prod_{s=2}^{T}p\!\left(z_{msj} \mid z_{m,s-1,j}\right)\prod_{s=1}^{T}p\!\left(\mathbf{y}_{msj}\mid z_{msj}\right),

with the probabilities

p(𝐲msj∣zmsj)={∏i=1nmf(ymisj)zmsj=1∏i=1nm𝟙[ymisj=0]zmsj=0 p\!\left(\mathbf{y}_{msj}\mid z_{msj}\right) = \begin{cases} \prod_{i=1}^{n_m} f\!\left(y_{misj}\right) & z_{msj} = 1\\[4pt] \prod_{i=1}^{n_m} \mathbb{1}\!\left[y_{misj}=0\right] & z_{msj} = 0 \end{cases}

In other words

survey ss survey s+1s+1 occupancy
seen seen definitely there
seen not seen could be there now
not seen seen could have been there before, definitely there now
not seen not seen honestly, no idea. It was not seen, but it could still be there

If a species was seen in a previous survey but is not seen now, it could have gone extinct, or it may have been missed. That means the observation is informative about the probability of local extinction, and apparent loss. If the absence cannot be explained by lack of cover from warming (given that altitude is constant through time), it could be due to local extinction after occupancy at the previous survey.

Similarly, if a presence cannot be explained by an increase in cover due to warming, it could be due to colonisation since the previous survey. In that sense, it is the model structure that separates warming effects on cover and occupancy. Because the probability of an absence in the ordered-beta model is derived from the same mean structure as cover (up to the cut-offs), the model cannot raise the probability of zeros across the environment without also lowering cover. That is how the dynamic occupancy model sorts out which information is due to which process.

Marginal likelihood

Occupancy is latent, so I need to integrate over the histories, which is a sum over the possible combinations. Each history is one path through the summit’s observations, so its terms are worth reading off survey by survey rather than as a product of two separate tables. At the first survey, the marginal is:

p(𝐲m1j)={ψmj∏i=1nmf(ymi1j)occupant with cover, if 𝐲m1j≠𝟎ψmj∏i=1nmpmi1j0occupant without cover, if 𝐲m1j=𝟎1−ψmjnot an occupant, so no cover, if 𝐲m1j=𝟎0if 𝐲m1j≠𝟎: somehow you managed to have cover but not occupancy, congratulations, you’ve broken statistics.. p\!\left(\mathbf{y}_{m1j}\right) = \begin{cases} \psi_{mj}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} f\!\left(y_{mi1j}\right) & \text{occupant with cover}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{m1j} \neq \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] \psi_{mj}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} p^{0}_{mi1j} & \text{occupant without cover}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{m1j} = \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] 1-\psi_{mj} & \text{not an occupant, so no cover}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{m1j} = \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] 0 & \text{if } \mathbf{y}_{m1j} \neq \mathbf{0}\text{: somehow you managed to have cover but not occupancy, congratulations, you've broken statistics.} \end{cases}. At the next survey, the probability that a species is an occupant is ψmjs=p(zmsj=1)\psi_{mjs} = p(z_{msj}=1)

ψmj1=ψmj,ψmjs=ψm,j,s−1ϕm,s−1+(1−ψm,j,s−1)γm,s−1, \psi_{mj1} = \psi_{mj}, \qquad \psi_{mjs} = \psi_{m,j,s-1}\,\phi_{m,s-1} + \left(1-\psi_{m,j,s-1}\right)\gamma_{m,s-1},

so that, marginalising over both states of occupancy at the previous survey, and the possible states at this survey, the marginal likelihood for survey ss is

p(𝐲msj)={ψm,j,s−1ϕm,s−1∏i=1nmf(ymisj)persistence with cover, if 𝐲msj≠𝟎ψm,j,s−1ϕm,s−1∏i=1nmpmisj0persistence without cover, if 𝐲msj=𝟎ψm,j,s−1(1−ϕm,s−1)extinction: occupant before but not now, if 𝐲msj=𝟎(1−ψm,j,s−1)γm,s−1∏i=1nmf(ymisj)occupant now but not before: colonisation, with cover, if 𝐲msj≠𝟎(1−ψm,j,s−1)γm,s−1∏i=1nmpmisj0occupant now but not before: colonisation, without cover, if 𝐲msj=𝟎(1−ψm,j,s−1)(1−γm,s−1)still absent, if 𝐲msj=𝟎0if 𝐲msj≠𝟎: somehow you managed to have cover but not occupancy, congratulations, you’ve broken statistics. p\!\left(\mathbf{y}_{msj}\right) = \begin{cases} \psi_{m,j,s-1}\,\phi_{m,s-1}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} f\!\left(y_{misj}\right) & \text{persistence with cover}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{msj} \neq \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] \psi_{m,j,s-1}\,\phi_{m,s-1}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} p^{0}_{misj} & \text{persistence without cover}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{msj} = \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] \psi_{m,j,s-1}\left(1-\phi_{m,s-1}\right) & \text{extinction: occupant before but not now}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{msj} = \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] \left(1-\psi_{m,j,s-1}\right)\gamma_{m,s-1}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} f\!\left(y_{misj}\right) & \text{occupant now but not before: colonisation, with cover}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{msj} \neq \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] \left(1-\psi_{m,j,s-1}\right)\gamma_{m,s-1}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} p^{0}_{misj} & \text{occupant now but not before: colonisation, without cover}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{msj} = \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] \left(1-\psi_{m,j,s-1}\right)\left(1-\gamma_{m,s-1}\right) & \text{still absent}\text{, if } \mathbf{y}_{msj} = \mathbf{0}\\[4pt] 0 & \text{if } \mathbf{y}_{msj} \neq \mathbf{0}\text{: somehow you managed to have cover but not occupancy, congratulations, you've broken statistics.} \end{cases}

For clarity, I have written out the cases with and without cover, even though they will look similar to the model in terms of occupancy. An absence for species jj occurs without cover in any plot with probability f(0)=pmisj0f(0) = p^{0}_{misj}. This probability has the same form as when there is cover in a plot, except that it’s evaluated at zero cover in every plot. This is what separates lack of occupancy from occupancy without cover, since ∏ipmisj0\prod_i p^{0}_{misj} is the probability where the cover model accounts for absence, while entries with 1−ϕm,s−11-\phi_{m,s-1} (extinction) or 1−γm,s−11-\gamma_{m,s-1} (continued absence) are due to occupancy.

In this manner I could go through every term in the likelihood transparently, to get a feeling for how the histories in the data are reflected by the model. Note, this “marginal” likelihood omits the random effects terms for brevity.

How I fit the model

I wrote the negative log-likelihood in R and handed it to RTMB, for the Laplace approximation and automatic differentiation. RTMB returns the likelihood function and its gradient, which I handed to optim to estimate the parameters, using a branch of RTMB that runs the model in parallel (RTMBp).

optim uses quasi-Newton optimisation, which at best converges to a local optimum, not necessarily the global one. These implementations tend to be sensitive to starting values, which I generated from per-species fits of cover, so the model had to be fitted several times to find a well-converged fit, restarting it from the same starting values with some normally distributed jitter.

Confidence transitions and standard errors were calculated (usually by simulation) from the joint asymptotic covariance matrix of fixed and random effects returned by RTMB.

Retrieving results from this model

Here I briefly summarise the types of statistics I can get from the model. This is not exhaustive, but covers some of the quantities Wessely et al. show interest in: local extinction due to warming and apparent loss (the probability of the former is always lower than that of the latter, by design), colonisation, species richness (due to occupancy and due to detection, where the latter is always lower than the former), and the probability of particular histories, such as p(1→0)p(1\to0), p(1→0→0)p(1\to0\to0) and p(1→0→0→0)p(1\to0\to0\to0), the latent counterpart of the conservative accounting of Wessely et al.

The probability that species jj occupies summit mm at survey ss, ψmsj=p(zmsj=1)\psi_{msj} = p(z_{msj}=1), follows from the transition probabilities without conditioning on cover

ψm1j=ψmj,ψmsj=ψm,s−1,jϕm,s−1+(1−ψm,s−1,j)γm,s−1. \psi_{m1j} = \psi_{mj}, \qquad \psi_{msj} = \psi_{m,s-1,j}\,\phi_{m,s-1} + \left(1-\psi_{m,s-1,j}\right)\gamma_{m,s-1}.

The probability of a particular history, say p(1→0)p(1\to 0), is given by the Markov chain of the latent states, so that

p(zm,s−1,j=1,zmsj=0)=p(zm,s−1,j=1)p(zmsj=0∣zm,s−1,j=1)=ψm,s−1,j(1−ϕm,s−1).\begin{align*} p(z_{m,s-1,j} = 1, z_{msj} = 0) &= p(z_{m,s-1,j}=1)\,p(z_{msj} = 0\mid z_{m,s-1,j} = 1)\\ &= \psi_{m,s-1,j}(1-\phi_{m,s-1}). \end{align*}

Any following history is retrieved by multiplication with the transition probabilities, so p(1→0→0)=ψm,s−1,j(1−ϕm,s−1)(1−γm,s)p(1\to0\to0) = \psi_{m,s-1,j}(1-\phi_{m,s-1})(1-\gamma_{m,s}) and p(1→0→0→0)=ψm,s−1,j(1−ϕm,s−1)(1−γm,s)(1−γm,s+1)p(1\to0\to0\to0) = \psi_{m,s-1,j}(1-\phi_{m,s-1})(1-\gamma_{m,s})(1-\gamma_{m,s+1}) for continued absence, or p(1→0→0→1)=ψm,s−1,j(1−ϕm,s−1)(1−γm,s)γm,s+1p(1\to0\to0\to1) = \psi_{m,s-1,j}(1-\phi_{m,s-1})(1-\gamma_{m,s})\gamma_{m,s+1} for a species that recolonised by the last resurvey.

The probability of a presence (non-zero cover in a plot) is the probability of occupancy weighted by the probability that the cover process does not return a zero, 1−pmisj01-p^0_{misj}

p(ymisj>0)=ψmsj(1−pmisj0),p(y_{misj}>0) = \psi_{msj}(1-p^0_{misj}),

and the probability of being recorded somewhere on the summit is p(𝐲msj≠𝟎)=ψmsj(1−∏i=1nmpmisj0)p(\mathbf{y}_{msj}\neq\mathbf{0}) = \psi_{msj}\left(1-\prod_{i=1}^{n_m}p^0_{misj}\right). Recorded histories follow from the same Markov chain, by weighting each latent state with the probability of the observation.

Detected richness at a plot is the expected number of species with non-zero cover ∑j=1Jp(ymisj>0)\sum_{j=1}^{J}p(y_{misj}>0), and at a summit the same with the probability of being recorded in any plot. It is always less than occupancy richness, since some occupants do not have cover, i.e., ∑j=1Jp(ymisj>0)≤∑j=1Jψmsj\sum_{j=1}^{J}p(y_{misj}>0) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{J} \psi_{msj}, where the former probability is a function of the latter.

From this I can deduce the expected loss of species from one survey to the next. The expected number of species lost from summit mm between surveys s−1s-1 and ss is ∑j=1Jψm,s−1,j(1−ϕm,s−1)\sum_{j=1}^{J} \psi_{m,s-1,j}(1-\phi_{m,s-1}), while the difference ∑j=1Jψmsj−∑j=1Jψm,s−1,j\sum_{j=1}^{J} \psi_{msj} - \sum_{j=1}^{J} \psi_{m,s-1,j} is the net change, gains minus losses. Both are the same at plot level, as occupancy is a summit-level quantity. A detected loss at summit level needs the species to occur in a plot at survey s−1s-1 and not at survey ss, so the expected loss is the probability of being recorded at survey s−1s-1 times the probability of apparent loss at the summit, summed over species ∑j=1Jψm,s−1,j(1−∏i=1nmpmi,s−1,j0)[(1−ϕm,s−1)+ϕm,s−1∏i=1nmpmisj0]\sum_{j=1}^J \psi_{m,s-1,j}\left(1-\prod_{i=1}^{n_m}p^0_{mi,s-1,j}\right)\left[(1-\phi_{m,s-1}) + \phi_{m,s-1}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m}p^0_{misj}\right]. Expected losses across the whole study are calculated similarly.

4. Results

The following figure visualises local extinction and apparent loss against warming. The expected number of extinction events per summit is shown in solid lines and recorded losses in dashed lines. Faded lines represent draws from the asymptotic distribution of the estimates, so they may be wider than 95% confidence bands. Apparent losses are higher than local extinctions, which is expected by the form of the probability, as it is the probability of extinction plus the probability of persistence and non-detection.

Expected number of species per summit going extinct (latent, solid) and recorded as lost (dashed), per transition, against the warming over that transition.

The main things to note are:

  • warming increases local extinction as in Wessely et al. table S5. More on that in Section 5;
  • the uncertainty is larger than for Wessely et al. (SE 0.16 against 0.08 in their table S5), a natural consequence of incorporating the variation due to species heterogeneity;
  • omitting the frequency method results in more zeros, as indicated by a positive δFζ\delta^{\zeta}_F;
  • the level of local extinction is far below their apparent loss. Their summit-level intercept in table S5 is −2.49, against −6.10 from the dynamic occupancy model, but the two are not on the same scale. Theirs is the logit of the probability of not being re-observed in a transition, at the mean warming over all transitions, and this model’s the log of the annual extinction rate at the mean warming of the first survey. Over a transition of on average 6.9 years and at their mean warming, this model’s corresponds to −6.10 + 0.42 × 0.68 + log 6.9 = −3.88, and for probabilities this small the log and logit scales nearly coincide. That is expected, as the probability of apparent loss (section 3) is the probability of extinction plus the probability of persistence multiplied by the probability of being missed in every plot;
  • there is insufficient evidence to conclude that colonisation changes with warming, as in Wessely et al. table S11, with again higher uncertainty. Their intercept is 1.06 against −8.20 here. Over a transition of on average 6.9 years and at their mean warming, this model’s corresponds to −8.20 + 0.12 × 0.68 + log 6.9 = −6.18. Theirs is not on this scale either. It is the log of the number of apparent colonisations on a summit rather than the logit of a probability per species, so it also contains the log of the number of species absent from the summit, and the two cannot be compared directly.

For comparison, the following figure shows local extinction from the model in blue, and the summit-level regression of apparent loss from table S5 of Wessely et al. in black.

Summit-level apparent loss as published (black, table S5 of Wessely et al.) and local extinction from this model (blue), against warming. Bands are 95% confidence intervals: theirs from the table S5 standard errors, taking intercept and slope as uncorrelated because their predictor is centred and no covariance is given; this model’s from the joint draws.

Although there are significant differences, the warming slopes are comparable, so that the difference is mainly in the intercept.

Wessely et al. report counts of transitions, and I can predict similar quantities from the model.

Their per-transition count is 118 to 185 summit-level extinction events per resurvey (p. 1021); this includes species observed on a summit and not observed at the next survey. For the species in the analysis here, the data has 96, 140 and 128 such losses in the three transitions, 364 in total. Given the species observed at the survey before, the model predicts 393, about as many, but only 140 of them (36%) are extinctions. The other 253 are species that persisted and were missed. Among all occupants, including those that were not observed at the survey before and so cannot show up as a loss, the model predicts 184 local extinctions over the three transitions, about half the 364 observed losses. The model predicts far more false absences than unobserved extinctions.

Their “most conservative accounting”, 62 summit-level extinction events (p. 1021), counts species observed on a summit at the first survey and at none of the three that follow (all species, before filtering the data). For the species here, the data has 50 of these. Starting from the species observed at the first survey, the model predicts 49, close to the observed 50, but only 38 of them are true 1→0→0→01\to0\to0\to0 histories. In case of the other 11 events, species persisted to the second survey and were missed from then on, or went extinct later. At the same time, 12 of the 49 true 1→0→0→01\to0\to0\to0 histories in the model belong to species that were not observed at the first survey, so they cannot appear in the count. The observed 50 is close to the 49 true histories only because these two statistics effectively cancel out. Of the 49 observed 1,0,0,01,0,0,0 histories predicted by the model, about 23% belong to species that did not go extinct in the first transition. About as many species that did go extinct in it are not among them, because they were not observed at the first survey. In contrast, in the liberal accounting the false absences are about double.

The extinction rate is a ratio over observed species, so it is inflated by false absences. The count also loses the extinctions of species that were never observed, so whether it is too high or too low depends on the accounting. Further, a species that persisted but was missed may turn up again in a later survey, as an apparent colonisation, which moves its history out of the conservative count and into the other histories. An observed history of 1,0,11,0,1 is therefore not evidence of recolonisation either.

5. Simulations

So, if analysing apparent loss to infer local extinction is a poor idea, why did the analysis of Wessely et al. estimate an effect of warming on local extinction so similar to that of the dynamic occupancy model?

I have established that the probability of apparent loss is due to both the extinction process and the cover process. That means that the way species’ cover responds to warming, and the way extinction responds to warming, both affect the warming signal in apparent loss. I may have given away my conclusion here, but bear with me.

The model can estimate the response of cover and the response of local extinction to warming separately, because, as in section 3, the cover model can only make zeros more likely by also lowering cover. It has limited flexibility to explain zeros that are not due to the cover process (i.e., local extinction), because that would require sacrificing fit to the cover data. That does not mean that the two cannot move in similar directions anyway, they just do not need to.

For a species recorded on a summit, the probability of an apparent loss is (1−ϕm,s−1)+ϕm,s−1∏i=1nmpmisj0(1-\phi_{m,s-1}) + \phi_{m,s-1}\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} p^0_{misj} (section 3). It is driven by extinction, or persistence and being missed in every plot. Warming can move apparent loss via ϕm,s−1\phi_{m,s-1} through extinction, and ∏i=1nmpmisj0\prod_{i=1}^{n_m} p^0_{misj} through cover. The warming signal in apparent loss is therefore a mix of the two. So what is necessary for the warming signal in apparent loss (what Wessely et al. analyse) to be similar to that in local extinction? The authors argue that “if all local extinctions were attributable to observer errors or random fluctuation, significant relationships with time, level of warming, or relative elevational rank should not emerge” (p. 1025). That requires the cover process to be independent of time, warming and elevation, but being missed does depend on cover, as they themselves established.

Here I simulate from the fitted model (so the parameters estimated from the data are taken as true baseline that I simulate from), but change the distribution of species responses to warming for cover relative to what was estimated from the data, in order to explore how that affects the relationship of apparent loss with warming. For simplicity, I omit the altitude terms in cover. Changing the responses also requires an adjustment of the cut-off parameters, to keep the simulated data similar to the fitted model. I do not change anything in the parameter estimates from the data for initial occupancy.

The fitted warming slopes for cover. The average response of cover to warming is slightly negative.

Initial occupancy is propagated in the simulation with the extinction and colonisation rates at the fitted βext\beta^{\mathrm{ext}} and βcol\beta^{\mathrm{col}}, using each summit’s warming and resurvey times, with the random effects on extinction and colonisation set to zero, so that extinction responds to warming with exactly the fitted slope estimate. A species present on the summit is recorded in a plot with probability 1−pmisj01-p^0_{misj}, from the fitted species intercepts and cut-offs and the fitted survey and sampling-method intercept, so the continuous part of cover need not be simulated to analyse apparent loss.

Every simulation is analysed as in Wessely et al., with a binomial GLMM for the species recorded on a summit that were not re-recorded at the next survey, with warming as predictor, with random intercepts for region and summit within region. The estimated slope parameter is on the scale of Wessely et al. table S5, per standard deviation of warming. The true parameter is β1ext=\beta^{\mathrm{ext}}_1 = 0.42 per standard deviation of warming on the log-rate scale, as reported in section 4. Each scenario is simulated 50 times, and the tables report the means of estimates from the simulations.

I include eight scenarios:

  1. Cut-offs and the mean species responses to warming adjusted so that the binomial GLMM returns a result similar to the analysis of Wessely et al.. The fitted distribution of responses is moved to a mean of −0.40 (against −0.05 fitted), and the cut-offs are lowered by 0.92;
  2. Species responses to warming are made more negative. The fitted distribution is moved to a mean of −1.00, with the cut-offs of scenario 1;
  3. Only cut-offs are adjusted as in scenario 1, but with the fitted responses to warming from the fitted model. These have a mean of −0.05, with 63% of species negative, and the cut-offs lowered by 0.92;
  4. No response from cover to warming, so that species responses to warming for cover are zero, but the warming effect on local extinction is kept, with the cut-offs of scenario 1;
  5. The opposite of scenario 1, so that species responses to warming are positive on average. The fitted distribution is moved to a mean of +0.40, with the cut-offs of scenario 1;
  6. Species responses to warming are made more positive. The fitted distribution is moved to a mean of +1.00, with the cut-offs of scenario 1;
  7. As scenario 6, but the cut-offs are adjusted up to match richness. They are raised by 1.67 from the fitted ones, so that the simulated data has 10.0 species per plot, as the observed data;
  8. The fitted responses to warming but the cut-offs are lowered to minimise absences due to cover, by 20.

The estimated intercept and slope are those the analysis of Wessely et al. returns, on the logit scale, per standard deviation of warming as in table S5, averaged over the simulations. The true slope is β1ext\beta^{\mathrm{ext}}_1, on the log-rate scale per standard deviation of warming. The true intercept is the intercept the same analysis returns when applied to the true extinctions instead, so it is on the scale of the estimated intercept; β0ext\beta^{\mathrm{ext}}_0 is a log annual rate at the warming of the first survey, and is not. For probabilities as small as these, the logit and log scales nearly coincide, so the estimated and true slopes are comparable.

Scenario 1 is calibrated to table S5. With species responses of cover to warming at a mean of −0.40, the analysis of Wessely et al. returns an intercept of −2.50 and a slope of 0.40, against −2.49 and 0.37 in table S5, and against a true intercept of −3.87 and a true slope of 0.42. The slope is nearly right because absences due to cover rise with warming at about the rate extinction does, not because apparent loss measures extinction. As in the analysis of the real data, the intercept lies above the true intercept, in every scenario but scenario 8.

Scenario 8 is a benchmark, because with the cut-offs so low that the cover process almost never produces an absence, there is no dilution from the cover process, and the analysis of Wessely et al. recovers the true intercept (−3.87 against −3.87) and the true slope (0.40 against 0.42).

Scenarios 2 to 6 use the cut-offs of scenario 1, with other cover responses to warming. Because warming is centred on the first survey, changing the responses also changes average cover at the later surveys, and with it the number of absences due to cover. Across these scenarios detected richness ranges from 9.5 to 25.1 species per plot, against 10.0 observed. More negative responses than in scenario 1 (scenario 2), at a mean cover response of −1.00, give an estimated slope of 0.99, well above the truth. With no cover response (scenario 4) the estimated slope is 0.18, under half the truth. Extinction is the only part of apparent loss that responds to warming, and the false absences water down the signal, so the slope is underestimated. With the fitted cover responses (scenario 3) the estimated slope is 0.23, slightly above the 0.18 without a cover response, since the fitted responses are slightly negative on average. With responses that are positive on average (scenario 5), the estimated slope is 0.13, below the 0.18 without a cover response, as absences due to cover become rarer with warming, which pulls it down. More positive responses (scenario 6) give 0.14, no lower than in scenario 5. Once cover at the warm summits is high enough that absences due to cover are rare, there are few false absences left to remove, so the slope stops falling.

With higher cut-offs than in scenario 6, and so more absences due to cover, the same cover responses reverse the sign. With the cut-offs raised until the simulated data has as many species per plot as the observed data (scenario 7), the estimate is −0.45, for the truth at 0.42. The analysis of Wessely et al. would have concluded that warming reduces local extinction.

Without local extinction responding to warming, when most species’ cover reduces with warming, the analysis of Wessely et al. returns an effect of warming on extinction that is not there. The only exceptions are when the mean response of cover to warming is about zero (scenarios 3 and 4), and when the cover process almost never produces an absence (scenario 8).

The analysis returns 0.28 in scenario 1, and 0.99 in scenario 2. When most species respond positively to warming it returns a negative effect, from −0.11 (scenario 5) to −0.64 (scenario 7).

6. Summary and conclusion

In this document I reanalysed the GLORIA resurvey data of Wessely et al. with a dynamic occupancy model for cover. The model treats the occupancy of a summit as latent, and lets it change through extinction and colonisation at rates that depend on warming. A recorded zero can come from an occupant whose cover falls below the lower cut-off, or from a species that is not on the summit, and the model estimates the probability of each. Cover, occupancy, extinction and colonisation are jointly modelled, with species-specific intercepts partially pooled and species-specific slopes where the data allows them. I then simulated data from the fitted model, analysed the outcome following Wessely et al., and changed species responses to warming and the cut-offs, in the cover model, to find out what affects an analysis of apparent loss.

There are four main findings. First, local extinction increases with warming, as in Wessely et al., by 0.42 (SE 0.16) per standard deviation of warming on the log-rate scale, against their summit-level 0.37 (SE 0.08) on the logit scale. The standard error here is twice theirs, because the model incorporates the variation due to species heterogeneity that their analysis leaves out. Second, the model estimates local extinction to be much rarer than apparent loss. About 3.0% of occupants go extinct per transition, against an apparent loss of about 7% in the data, and a summit holds about 35 occupant species, of which about 27 were recorded at the first survey. Third, Wessely et al. report two counts of extinction events. The liberal count is of species recorded at one survey and not at the next, and the conservative count is of species recorded at the first survey and at none of the later ones. Both are counts of apparent loss, not of local extinctions. The model predicts about half as many local extinctions as the liberal count, and that about 23% of the conservative count consists of species that were still there at the second survey, but went undetected in later surveys. Fourth, the estimate of warming on apparent loss depends on how the species’ cover responds to warming, and the detection threshold. With a true response of local extinction to warming of 0.42, analysing apparent loss can return anything between −0.45 and 0.99 per standard deviation of warming, and anything between −0.64 and 0.99 when extinction does not respond to warming at all.

The same message echos through this reanalysis: local extinction should not be studied directly from apparent loss. A species that persists but is not detected produces apparent loss without extinction, so apparent loss overstates local extinction. A species that is never detected cannot be lost, so the published counts miss the local extinctions among undetected species. And because whether a species is detected depends on its cover, and cover depends on warming, apparent loss responds to warming for reasons that have nothing to do with extinction. This also holds for their analysis of apparent loss at the fourth survey against the change in cover (p. 1023), which cannot separate local extinction from the observation errors they mention themselves.

This reanalysis can be improved, mostly with by more data. Information on observers and effort per plot, and repeated visits within a survey, would let a model distinguish between a species that disappeared from a plot from one that was undetected in it. Traits that index cold against warm adaptation would let the extinction rate differ between species without 549 free parameters.

The analysis of Wessely et al. recovers the intercept and the slope only when the cover process almost never produces an absence. It recovers the slope alone when absences due to cover rise with warming at about the rate extinction does, and when neither responds to warming. When cover declines with warming more steeply, absences due to cover rise faster than extinction, and the slope is overestimated, to more than twice the truth. When cover does not respond to warming, or rises with it, absences due to cover dilute the extinction signal, and the slope is underestimated, to as little as a third of the truth. When cover rises with warming and the cut-offs give the observed number of species per plot, the sign reverses, and local extinction would be inferred to decline with warming. Without an extinction response, a decline of cover with warming produces an effect of warming on extinction that is not there, and a rise produces a negative effect.

Why go to the trouble of a joint model? Because richness, extinction and cover are summaries of the same data, and analysing them separately does not utilise the shared structure in the data, and what the different aspects of the data can inform about each other. In a joint model a recorded zero has to be explained either by the cover process or by occupancy, and the cover model would have to sacrifice its estimates of cover to produce zeros that do not fit the process, so such zeros are attributed to occupancy.

Still, I found the same effect of warming on local extinction as Wessely et al. The dynamic occupancy model also estimates warming raises local extinction on these summits, by 0.42 per standard deviation of warming (95% CI 0.11 to 0.73). However, what this analysis has made apparent is that the result is the same as that of Wessely et al. not because it could be expected a priori, but by luck of the draw. Had the species’ cover responded to warming more negatively or more positively on average, their analysis could have yielded a very different outcome. Apparent loss measures a change in the observations rather than a change in occupancy.

A regression will return a coefficient for whatever response it is given. Whether the coefficient means anything depends on whether the model reflects the process that produced the data. A model informed by the ecology, with realistic and stated assumptions, can be wrong in ways that can at least be predicted.
